drills.title: Sticky hex manipulator
drills.promptMd: Both `a` and `b` are ordinary ints. What does this program print?
drills.explanationMd: `std::hex` is a *sticky* manipulator: once streamed into `std::cout`, every subsequent integer prints in hexadecimal until you explicitly switch back with `std::dec`. So both `a` (255 → `ff`) and `b` (16 → `10`) are printed in hex. The common mistake is assuming each output statement resets to decimal on its own — it does not.

drills.title: constexpr with a non-constexpr function
drills.promptMd: What happens when you compile this program?
drills.explanationMd: `constexpr` requires its initializer to be a *constant expression* — something the compiler can fully evaluate during compilation. `getMax()` is a plain (non-`constexpr`) function, so its return value is only known at runtime. The compiler rejects the initializer with an error. If you want `limit` to be a compile-time constant, you would mark `getMax()` as `constexpr` — or just write the literal directly.

drills.title: Fix the name-builder
drills.promptMd: The function is supposed to return `"First Last"` but produces only the last name. Find and fix the single-character mistake.
drills.explanationMd: `result = last` *replaces* the entire string with the last name, discarding the first name and space that were built up before it. The fix is `result += last`, which *appends* to what is already in `result`. This is a one-character difference (`=` vs `+=`) that completely changes meaning — a classic source of subtle build-string bugs.

drills.title: Octal literal masquerading as decimal
drills.promptMd: The function is supposed to classify codes below 100 as `"small"` and codes 100 or above as `"large"`, but the threshold is wrong. Find the bug.
drills.explanationMd: A leading `0` makes an integer literal *octal*. `0100` is octal 100, which equals decimal 64 — not the intended 100. So the threshold was 64, causing codes like 64–99 to be misclassified as `"large"`. The fix is simply `100` without the leading zero. This is why the chapter warns to avoid accidental leading zeros: `012` is not twelve, `0100` is not one hundred.

drills.title: Build a badge label with constexpr and string_view
drills.promptMd: Implement `badgeLabel` and `badgeLabelLength` using the provided `constexpr` prefix constant and `std::string_view` parameters.
drills.explanationMd: `constexpr std::string_view` is the idiomatic compile-time string constant: `constexpr` guarantees the value is known at compile time, and `string_view` owns nothing so there is no runtime allocation. To build the result you seed an owning `std::string` from the view (`std::string result { kPrefix }`) and append with `+=`. `.length()` returns an unsigned `size_t`, so the cast `static_cast<int>(...)` makes the arithmetic signed and warning-free.
